blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. Choose **one** day to buy a share and a **later** day to sell it. Return the largest profit you can make — or `0` if no trade makes money.

blocks.alt: A line chart of prices [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] over days 0 to 5. Buying at price 1 on day 1 and selling at price 6 on day 4 gives the largest profit, 5.

elements.text: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
elements.originalText: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

blocks.code:
Input:  prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
Output: 5     buy on day 1 (price 1), sell on day 4 (price 6)

Input:  prices = [7, 6, 4, 3, 1]
Output: 0     the price only falls, so don't trade

blocks.text: You need two days, `buy < sell`, that make `prices[sell] - prices[buy]` as large as possible. The order matters: in the first example the highest price is 7, but it comes **before** the lowest price, so you can't buy at 1 and sell at 7.
If every possible trade loses money, you simply don't trade — the answer is 0, never negative.
Brute force: try every pair of days
Every pair is checked, so this is **O(n²)** — about 5 billion comparisons for 100,000 days.
The key insight: remember the cheapest day so far
Flip the question around. Instead of asking "when should I buy?", pretend **today** is the day you sell. Then the best day to have bought is simply the **cheapest day before today**.

So walk through the days once, carrying two numbers: `minPrice`, the cheapest price seen so far, and `maxProfit`, the best sale found so far. On each day, selling today would earn `price - minPrice`; if that beats `maxProfit`, keep it.

blocks.alt: A table over days 0 to 5. Prices: 7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4. Cheapest so far: 7, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Profit if sold today: 0, 0, 4, 2, 5, 3. Best profit so far: 0, 0, 4, 4, 5, 5.
blocks.caption: Each column only needs the column before it — that's why one pass is enough.

blocks.text: The bars show the price on each day. Watch `min` move to every new low, and `maxProfit` grow only when selling today beats the best so far.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n²) time and O(1) space. One pass: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: Each day is looked at once: **O(n) time, O(1) space**.

items: **One day** — `[5]` returns 0; you can't buy and sell on the same day.
**The best buy comes late** — `[3, 8, 2, 9]`: buying at 2 and selling at 9 beats buying at 3.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

This is Kadane's algorithm in disguise: the profit of a trade is the sum of the day-to-day price changes between buying and selling, so the best trade is the maximum subarray of those changes. Follow-ups change the rules — unlimited trades (add up every rise), at most two trades, or a cooldown day — and lead into dynamic programming.
